SEQ Transit AI predicts delays on the Gold Coast to Brisbane corridor. TransLink publishes system-wide monthly on-time averages, but no stop-level or per-line delay history, so I built the sensor first: an archiver on EC2 polls the GTFS-Realtime feeds every five minutes and stores them in S3, which gave me 156 million rows across 46 days. An XGBoost model trained on that archive has a test MAE of 1.957 minutes against a 2.486-minute naive baseline, a 21.3% improvement. When it meets a stop it hasn't seen in training, it forces the confidence label to Low, because a wrong answer that looks confident is worse than no answer. It runs on AWS (EC2, S3, CloudFront) with a FastAPI back end and a Leaflet map. Try it at d17e9wvem3lbaq.cloudfront.net. The code is at github.com/proteek-dev/Transit-AI.

The Automated Scheme Research Tool is a retrieval-augmented assistant. Government schemes go unused because the details sit in long pages nobody reads. You give it scheme URLs, LangChain loads the pages, SentenceTransformers embeds them, and a FAISS index finds the passage closest to your question. DistilBERT extracts the answer, and the Streamlit chat shows it with its source URL and a short summary. It runs on free Hugging Face models, because a tool that only works with a paid API key isn't much use to the organisations that need it most. The code is at github.com/proteek-dev/ASRT, and there's a write-up on my Medium.

qa.topic: Maternal Health and Early Outbreak Warning
response: Maternal Health and Early Outbreak Warning is an open-source prototype, prompted by the UNCTAD white paper on AI for Good. It screens maternal health risk factors and flags unusual spikes in reported community symptoms. I used logistic regression and z-score anomaly detection on purpose, because a health worker has to be able to understand why a case was flagged. I documented it as a prototype, not production software. The code is at github.com/proteek-dev/Maternal-Health-Early-Warning, and there's a write-up on my Medium.

response: The decision I'd point to is in SEQ Transit AI. When the model meets a stop it hasn't seen in training, it forces the confidence label to Low, even when the prediction looks clean. A wrong answer that looks confident is worse than no answer.

qa.topic: why the health project uses simple models
response: For Maternal Health and Early Outbreak Warning I used logistic regression and z-score anomaly detection, nothing more sophisticated. A health worker has to be able to understand why a case was flagged, and it has to run on a laptop or low-cost cloud.

qa.topic: how he collected the transit data
triggers: how did you get the data
response: I built the sensor first. TransLink publishes system-wide monthly on-time averages, but no stop-level or per-line delay history. So an archiver on EC2 polls TransLink's GTFS-Realtime feeds every five minutes and stores them in S3, including the tram endpoints the combined feed leaves out. That gave me 156 million rows across 46 days.

qa.topic: what his projects don't do yet
response: SEQ Transit AI: tram data is still thin, so tram predictions carry lower confidence. Live delay isn't blended into the production prediction yet; that's the next model version. Ferry is excluded on purpose. The Automated Scheme Research Tool retrieves a single best passage per question, and the summary is a short extract from that passage. Next is categorising schemes by topic and updating the index as new URLs are added. Maternal Health and Early Outbreak Warning is a prototype trained and tested on synthetic data. It hasn't been clinically validated, and encryption, hashed identifiers and bias testing are listed as prerequisites before anyone takes it further.
